subject: mathematics_1b
question_text: Show that the function f, defined by f(x) = (cos ax − cos bx)/x² for x ≠ 0 and f(0) = (1/2)(b² − a²), where a and b are real constants, is continuous at x = 0.

recall_prompt: Say how you would do this one — say what continuity at 0 asks you to check, and name the identity and the standard limit you would use to get the limit.

steps.label: State the continuity test at 0
steps.margin_note: First mark. Write the test as lim(x → 0) f(x) = f(0) before any algebra. At x = 0 the quotient is the indeterminate form 0/0, so the limit has to be worked out and cannot be reached by substituting 0.
steps.memory_tip: Continuity at a point is three things in one line: the limit exists, the value exists, and the two are equal.
lines: Given f(x) = (cos ax − cos bx)/x²   for x ≠ 0,
and f(0) = ½(b² − a²)
(the definition of continuity at a point: the limit exists
f is continuous at x = 0 if   lim(x → 0) f(x) = f(0)
One single formula covers both sides of 0,
so one two-sided limit is enough.
(cos 0 − cos 0 = 1 − 1 = 0 and 0² = 0)
Putting x = 0 in (cos ax − cos bx)/x² gives 0/0,
an indeterminate form, so the limit must be worked out.

recall.must_convey: That continuity at 0 means lim(x → 0) f(x) must equal f(0), and that direct substitution gives 0/0.
accept: continuity at zero means the limit equals f of zero
check whether the limit as x tends to zero is the same as f zero
state the test first, limit equals value
limit x tends to zero, f of zero ki samanam avvali
substituting zero gives zero by zero so the limit has to be worked

steps.why: Naming the test first splits the question into two separate pieces of work — find the limit, then compare it with the given value — and each piece carries its own marks.
common_mistakes: Checking only that f(0) exists and stopping there.
Substituting x = 0 into (cos ax − cos bx)/x² and writing 0 as the limit.

steps.label: Change the difference of cosines to a product
steps.margin_note: Second mark. Name the identity as you use it. The order (D − C)/2 inside the second sine is what fixes the sign, and the sign decides whether the answer comes out (b² − a²)/2 or its negative.
steps.memory_tip: Two cosines subtracted give two sines multiplied, and the second sine takes the second angle first: (D − C)/2.
lines: For x ≠ 0,   f(x) = (cos ax − cos bx)/x²

lines.text: (the usual form is cos C − cos D

lines: Use the identity
cos C − cos D = 2 sin((C + D)/2) · sin((D − C)/2)
Take C = ax and D = bx. Then
cos ax − cos bx = 2 sin((a + b)x/2) · sin((b − a)x/2)
∴ f(x) = 2 sin((a + b)x/2) · sin((b − a)x/2) / x²

recall.must_convey: That cos C − cos D is rewritten as 2 sin((C + D)/2) sin((D − C)/2) with C = ax and D = bx.
accept: use the cos C minus cos D identity to make it a product of two sines
change the difference of cosines into two sines multiplied
cos ax minus cos bx is two sin of a plus b x by two into sin of b minus a x by two
cosines difference ni product ga marchali
apply the sum to product formula for the two cosines

steps.why: The product form puts one sine above for each factor of x below, which is exactly the shape the standard sine limit needs. The difference of cosines has no such shape.
common_mistakes: Writing cos C − cos D = 2 sin((C + D)/2) sin((C − D)/2), which reverses the sign of the answer.
Using the sum formula for cos C + cos D instead of the difference formula.
lines_compact: For x ≠ 0,   f(x) = (cos ax − cos bx)/x²
cos C − cos D = 2 sin((C + D)/2) · sin((D − C)/2)
Take C = ax and D = bx. Then
cos ax − cos bx = 2 sin((a + b)x/2) · sin((b − a)x/2)
∴ f(x) = 2 sin((a + b)x/2) · sin((b − a)x/2) / x²

steps.label: Apply the standard sine limit
steps.margin_note: Third mark. Each bracket is written in the exact form sin(angle)/(same angle) before the standard limit is quoted. The constants taken outside give (b² − a²)/2.
steps.memory_tip: sin(kx)/x tends to k, not to 1 — the constant multiplying x comes outside.

lines.text: (write x² = x · x and give one x to each sine)

lines: lim(x → 0) f(x) = lim(x → 0) 2 · [sin((a + b)x/2) / x]

lines.text: and the same for b − a; if a + b = 0 or b − a = 0,
then cos ax = cos bx, and both f(x) and the answer

lines: Multiply and divide the first bracket by (a + b)/2
and the second by (b − a)/2:
Standard limit:   lim(θ → 0) (sin θ)/θ = 1,
so each bracket tends to 1

recall.must_convey: That each sine is matched to its own angle so lim(θ → 0) (sin θ)/θ = 1 applies, leaving 2 · ((a+b)/2) · ((b−a)/2) = (b² − a²)/2.
accept: make each bracket sine of the angle over the same angle and use sin theta by theta equals one
multiply and divide by half of a plus b and half of b minus a
the standard limit sin theta by theta is one gives b squared minus a squared by two
sin theta by theta equals one use chesi constants bayata teeyali
the constants come out and both sine brackets become one
heard_as: b squared minus a squared by two

steps.why: The standard limit lim(θ → 0) (sin θ)/θ = 1 applies only when the angle inside the sine is the same as the expression below it, so each bracket has to be adjusted to that exact form first.
common_mistakes: Quoting sin θ/θ = 1 without first making the denominator match the angle.
Losing the factor 2 that came out of the cosine identity.
lines_compact: Multiply and divide the first bracket by (a + b)/2

steps.label: Compare the limit with f(0)
steps.margin_note: Last mark. Write the comparison line in full. A student who finds the limit and never says that it equals f(0) has not answered the question that was asked.
steps.memory_tip: The final line of every continuity proof is the same sentence: limit equals value, so f is continuous there.
lines: From above,   lim(x → 0) f(x) = (b² − a²)/2
It is given that   f(0) = ½(b² − a²) = (b² − a²)/2

recall.must_convey: That the limit (b² − a²)/2 equals the given f(0), so f is continuous at 0.
accept: the limit equals the given value so f is continuous at zero
b squared minus a squared by two is exactly f of zero
limit and value match so it is continuous
limit and f of zero rendu same, so continuous
compare the limit with the given f zero and they agree

steps.why: The question is answered by comparing two numbers: the limit that was computed and the value that was given. They are equal, so the definition of continuity is met.
common_mistakes: Stopping at the limit and never writing the comparison with f(0).
Reading ½(b² − a²) as ½b² − a².
lines_compact: It is given that   f(0) = ½(b² − a²) = (b² − a²)/2

insider_note: One formula covers both sides of 0, so a single two-sided limit is enough — no separate left and right work is needed. The limit comes to (b² − a²)/2, which is exactly the given f(0).
